subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9. In this unit you will learn to see the hidden rules behind patterns of numbers, and to describe those rules with the powerful language of algebra. A pattern like 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 is called a sequence, and instead of adding four again and again to reach the hundredth term, you will learn a single formula that jumps straight to any term you want. This idea, the nth term, is one of the most useful tools in all of school mathematics.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Understand term-to-term rules, and generate sequences from numerical and spatial patterns (including fractions).
Recognise that equations of the form y = mx + c correspond to straight-line graphs, where m is the gradient and c is the y-intercept (integer values of m).
Use knowledge of coordinate pairs to construct tables of values and plot the graphs of linear functions, where y is given explicitly in terms of x (y = mx + c).
Understand and describe nth term rules algebraically (in the form n ± a, a × n, or an ± b, where a and b are positive or negative integers or fractions).

Understand that a function is a relationship where each input has a single output. Generate outputs from a given function and identify inputs from a given output by considering inverse operations (including fractions).
Estimate and subtract mixed numbers, and write the answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.

outcomes: Identify and continue number sequences using term-to-term rules.
Find and use the nth term formula (of the form an + b) for linear sequences.
Generate sequences from a first term and a rule, including multi-step rules.
Connect visual patterns to numerical sequences and find their formulas.
Use function machines and write functions in the notation f(x) = ….
Build a table of values for a function and evaluate it for any input.
Draw and read the straight-line graph of a linear function.
Solve real-world problems, including finding when a sequence reaches a value or whether a number belongs to a sequence.

concepts.title: Sequences and Term-to-Term Rules
concepts.explanation:
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follows a rule. Each number is called a term, and its place in the line is its position: the first term, the second term, and so on. Look at the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, … The first term is 2, the second term is 5, the third term is 8. The three dots at the end mean the sequence carries on forever, following the same rule.

The term-to-term rule tells you how to move from one term to the next. For 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 the rule is “add 3”, because 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 + 3 = 8, then 8 + 3 = 11, and so on. A sequence that goes up or down by the same fixed amount every step is called a linear sequence (or arithmetic sequence), and that fixed amount is the common difference.

Sequences can also go down. Take 20, 17, 14, 11, 8, … Here the rule is “subtract 3”, so the common difference is −3. To find any common difference, subtract a term from the one after it: 17 − 20 = −3. If you always subtract the earlier term from the later term, a rising sequence gives a positive difference and a falling sequence gives a negative one.
concepts.example: When a sequence has gaps, use the rule to fill them. Consider 4, 9, __, 19, __, 29. First find the rule: 9 − 4 = 5, so it is “add 5”. The missing third term is 9 + 5 = 14, and the missing fifth term is 19 + 5 = 24. The complete sequence is 4, 9, 14, 19, 24, 29. Notice how one careful step at a time keeps you safe: find the rule, then apply it patiently to each gap.

concepts.title: The nth Term Formula
concepts.explanation:
The term-to-term rule is handy, but slow for large positions. To find the 100th term of 3, 7, 11, 15 you would have to add 4 ninety-nine times. The nth term formula fixes this. It is a rule that connects the position of a term (called n) directly to its value, so you can leap to any term at once. This is sometimes called the position-to-term rule.

For any linear sequence the nth term has the form an + b, where a is the common difference and b is a constant. The letter n stands for the position number: put n = 1 for the first term, n = 2 for the second, and so on. Let us find the formula for 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … step by step.

Step 1 — Find the common difference. 7 − 3 = 4, 11 − 7 = 4, so a = 4. The formula begins 4n.

Step 2 — Find b. When n = 1 the value must be 3. So 4(1) + b = 3, which gives 4 + b = 3, so b = −1.

Step 3 — Write the formula. nth term = 4n − 1.

Step 4 — Check. n = 2 gives 4(2) − 1 = 7 ✓; n = 3 gives 4(3) − 1 = 11 ✓.

A quick shortcut for b: once you know a, work out b = first term − a. For our sequence, b = 3 − 4 = −1, exactly as before. Always test your formula on two or three known terms before you trust it, because a small slip in b throws every term off by the same amount.
concepts.example: Now the power of the formula shows. To find the 50th term of 3, 7, 11, 15, you no longer add 4 fifty times. You simply substitute n = 50: nth term = 4(50) − 1 = 200 − 1 = 199. In one line you have reached a term that would take ages by hand. This is why the nth term is such a prized tool.

concepts.title: Generating Sequences and Multi-Step Rules
concepts.explanation:
You can also build a sequence forwards from a starting term and a rule. If you are told “first term = 5, rule = add 4”, you generate 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, … Generating a sequence from its nth term formula is just as easy: for nth term = 3n − 1, substitute n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 to get 2, 5, 8, 11, 14.

Some rules use more than one operation, and the order matters. Take “first term = 3, rule = multiply by 2, then subtract 1.” Starting at 3: the 2nd term is 3 × 2 − 1 = 5; the 3rd term is 5 × 2 − 1 = 9; the 4th term is 9 × 2 − 1 = 17. The sequence is 3, 5, 9, 17, … This is not linear, because the differences (2, 4, 8) are not constant. Multi-step rules can grow very fast.

Another example: “first term = 20, rule = divide by 2, then add 3.” We get 20, then 20 ÷ 2 + 3 = 13, then 13 ÷ 2 + 3 = 9.5, then 9.5 ÷ 2 + 3 = 7.75. The sequence is 20, 13, 9.5, 7.75, … Do not be alarmed by decimals; the rule is simply applied faithfully each step.
concepts.example: Sometimes you must work backwards to discover the rule from the sequence. Look at 8, 10, 14, 22, 38, … The differences are 2, 4, 8, 16 — they are doubling, which hints at a “multiply then add” rule. Testing “multiply by 2, then subtract 6”: 8 × 2 − 6 = 10 ✓, 10 × 2 − 6 = 14 ✓, 14 × 2 − 6 = 22 ✓. The rule works for every given term, so we can trust it. Always verify a proposed rule against all the terms you are given before using it.

concepts.title: Visual Patterns and Sequences
concepts.explanation:
Many sequences are born from pictures. Learning to count the pieces of a growing pattern in a systematic way lets you find the numerical sequence and then its formula. Imagine tiles laid out at Nuur Academy for a classroom display.

Consider an L-shaped tile pattern that grows: Pattern 1 uses 1 tile, Pattern 2 uses 3 tiles, Pattern 3 uses 5 tiles, Pattern 4 uses 7 tiles. The sequence is 1, 3, 5, 7, … — the odd numbers. The common difference is 2, so the formula begins 2n, and b = 1 − 2 = −1, giving nth term = 2n − 1. Check: n = 4 gives 2(4) − 1 = 7 ✓, matching the fourth pattern.

Square dot patterns give a different sequence. Pattern 1 is a single dot (1 = 1²), Pattern 2 is a 2-by-2 square (4 = 2²), Pattern 3 is a 3-by-3 square (9 = 3²). The nth pattern holds n² dots, so this is a square-number sequence: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Its differences are 3, 5, 7, 9 — not constant, so this sequence is not linear.
concepts.example: Triangle patterns build up like a stack: 1 dot, then 3 (1 + 2), then 6 (1 + 2 + 3), then 10 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4). These are the triangular numbers, and their formula is nth term = n(n + 1)/2. Check: for n = 4, 4 × 5 ÷ 2 = 10 ✓. The key skill in every visual pattern is to count the same way each time and record the totals as a sequence before you hunt for the rule.

concepts.title: Function Machines and Function Notation
concepts.explanation:
A function is a rule that takes an input, does something fixed to it, and produces exactly one output. A helpful picture is a function machine: a number goes in one end, the machine follows its rule, and a new number comes out the other end. If the machine’s rule is “× 2 then + 3”, then an input of 5 becomes 5 × 2 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13, so the output is 13.

Mathematicians write functions with function notation. We might name the machine f and write f(x) = 2x + 3. Here x is the input variable, the expression 2x + 3 is the rule, and f(x) is the output. The notation f(5) means “the output of f when the input is 5”. To evaluate it we substitute x = 5: f(5) = 2(5) + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13, exactly what the machine gave us.

Let us evaluate f(x) = 2x + 3 for more inputs so the idea is firm. f(1) = 2(1) + 3 = 5; f(4) = 2(4) + 3 = 11; and for a negative input, f(−2) = 2(−2) + 3 = −4 + 3 = −1. Take great care with the signs when the input is negative. A very common slip is to read f(3) as “f times 3”; it does not mean multiply. It means “the value of the function f at input 3”.
concepts.example: Functions describe the real world. The cost of a taxi in Kismaayo might be a base fare plus a charge for each kilometre: C(k) = 3 + 2k, where k is the number of kilometres and C is the cost in dollars. Converting a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit uses the function F(C) = 9C/5 + 32. In each case, one input gives exactly one output, which is the heart of what makes something a function.

concepts.title: Tables of Values and Linear Graphs
concepts.explanation:
A table of values lays out the inputs and outputs of a function side by side, which makes the relationship easy to see and to plot. For f(x) = 3x − 1 we choose some inputs and work out each output: when x = 0, f(x) = −1; when x = 1, f(x) = 2; when x = 2, f(x) = 5; when x = 3, f(x) = 8; when x = 4, f(x) = 11. Notice that each time x rises by 1, the output rises by 3 — the same as the coefficient of x. That steady step is the signature of a linear function.

Because the output climbs by the same amount for each equal step in the input, a linear function draws a perfectly straight line when you plot it. To draw the graph of y = 3x − 1, treat each pair from the table as a coordinate: (0, −1), (1, 2), (2, 5), (3, 8), (4, 11). Plot the points on a grid with x across and y up, then join them with a ruler. If the points do not lie in a straight line, check your arithmetic, because a linear function can never bend.

Two features of the line are worth naming. The point where the line crosses the vertical axis is the output when x = 0; for y = 3x − 1 that is (0, −1), and the number −1 is the constant in the rule. The steepness of the line, called its gradient, is the coefficient of x; for y = 3x − 1 the line climbs 3 for every 1 it moves to the right. So in a rule of the form y = mx + c, the m controls the slope and the c controls where the line crosses the vertical axis. This connects directly to the nth term form an + b you met earlier — the same linear idea in a new dress.
concepts.example: Graphs let you read off answers without algebra. If Halima plots the cost of internet data as y = 2x + 5 (a $5 fixed charge plus $2 per gigabyte), she can find the cost of any number of gigabytes by going up from that value on the x-axis to the line and across to the y-axis. Reading a graph both ways — input to output, and output back to input — is a skill you will use throughout mathematics and science.

methods.title: How to find an nth term formula
steps: Find the common difference a by subtracting one term from the next.
Write the formula as an, then work out b = first term − a.
Write the full formula an + b.
Check it gives the right value for two or three known terms.

methods.title: How to evaluate a function
steps: Write the rule with brackets where x appears.
Substitute the input in place of x.
Work out the arithmetic, taking care with negative inputs.
State the output clearly.

methods.title: How to draw a linear graph
methods.example: Draw the graph of y = 2x + 1 using a table of values for x = 0 to 4.
steps: Make a table of values for a few inputs.
Write each pair as a coordinate (x, y).
Plot the points on a grid.
Join them with a ruler and check they form a straight line.

methods.title: Generate a sequence with a two-step rule
methods.example: First term = 2, rule = “multiply by 3, then add 1”. Write the first four terms.
steps: Start at 2.

methods.title: Evaluate a function
methods.example: For f(x) = 3x + 7, find f(2), f(−1) and the value of x for which f(x) = 22.
steps: To solve f(x) = 22: 3x + 7 = 22, so 3x = 15, so x = 5.

methods.title: Complete a table of values
methods.example: Complete a table for g(x) = 2x − 5 using x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3.
steps: The outputs are −9, −7, −5, −3, −1, 1 — rising by 2 each step, so the graph would be a straight line.
Check by substituting one x-value back into the rule to confirm the output matches your table.

workedExamples.title: Continue a sequence and give the rule
workedExamples.prompt: Find the term-to-term rule and the next two terms of 6, 10, 14, 18, __, __.
workedExamples.solution: 10 − 6 = 4, so the rule is “add 4”. The next terms are 18 + 4 = 22 and 22 + 4 = 26. The sequence is 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 26.

workedExamples.title: Find the nth term formula
workedExamples.solution: Common difference a = 9 − 5 = 4, so the formula begins 4n. Then b = first term − a = 5 − 4 = 1. So nth term = 4n + 1. Check: n = 3 gives 4(3) + 1 = 13 ✓.

workedExamples.title: Use the formula to find a large term
workedExamples.prompt: Using nth term = 4n + 1, find the 20th term.
workedExamples.solution: Substitute n = 20: 4(20) + 1 = 80 + 1 = 81. No need to list all the terms — the formula jumps straight there.

workedExamples.title: Generate a sequence with a two-step rule
workedExamples.prompt: First term = 2, rule = “multiply by 3, then add 1”. Write the first four terms.
workedExamples.solution: Start at 2. Next: 2 × 3 + 1 = 7. Next: 7 × 3 + 1 = 22. Next: 22 × 3 + 1 = 67. The sequence is 2, 7, 22, 67. The differences grow, so it is not linear.

workedExamples.title: Evaluate a function
workedExamples.prompt: For f(x) = 3x + 7, find f(2), f(−1) and the value of x for which f(x) = 22.

workedExamples.title: Complete a table of values
workedExamples.prompt: Complete a table for g(x) = 2x − 5 using x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3.
workedExamples.solution: g(−2) = −9, g(−1) = −7, g(0) = −5, g(1) = −3, g(2) = −1, g(3) = 1. The outputs are −9, −7, −5, −3, −1, 1 — rising by 2 each step, so the graph would be a straight line.

workedExamples.title: First term over a target
workedExamples.prompt: In the sequence 4, 9, 14, 19, …, find the first term greater than 200.
workedExamples.solution: The formula is 5n − 1 (difference 5, b = 4 − 5 = −1). Set 5n − 1 > 200, so 5n > 201, so n > 40.2. Thus n = 41, and the 41st term is 5(41) − 1 = 204.

workedExamples.title: Model with a function
workedExamples.prompt: A gym charges $50 to join plus $15 per month. Write a function for the total cost after m months, find the cost after 8 months, and find when the total reaches $200.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: Complete the table of values for f(x) = 4x − 3 using x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3.
workedExamples.solution: f(−2) = −11, f(−1) = −7, f(0) = −3, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 5, f(3) = 9. The outputs rise by 4 each time, matching the coefficient of x.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: A student claims 6, 11, 16, 21, 26 has nth term 5n + 1. Check by substituting n = 1, 2, 3, and say whether the formula is correct.
workedExamples.solution: n = 1: 5(1) + 1 = 6 ✓. n = 2: 5(2) + 1 = 11 ✓. n = 3: 5(3) + 1 = 16 ✓. The formula 5n + 1 is correct — it matches every term.

workedExamples.title: Evaluate a linear function
workedExamples.prompt: For g(x) = 2x − 7, find a) g(5) b) g(−3) c) the value of x for which g(x) = 3.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Find the nth term of 12, 17, 22, 27, 32, … and use it to find the 100th term.

activities.title: Build a Growing Pattern
activities.materials: stones, bottle caps, matchsticks, or dry beans.
steps: Lay out an L-shape: 1 object, then 3, then 5, then 7, adding to the corner each time.
Write down the sequence of totals as you build each stage.
Find the common difference and write the nth term formula.
Predict the 10th stage with your formula, then build it to check you are right.
Try again with a square pattern (1, 4, 9, 16) and notice how the differences are not constant this time.

activities.title: The Function Machine Game
activities.materials: paper and a partner, or your AI tutor if no partner is available.
steps: Secretly choose a rule, for example “multiply by 2, then add 1”.
Ask your partner (or your AI tutor) for inputs and give back only the outputs.
Your partner or AI tutor keeps a table of inputs and outputs and tries to guess your rule.
Swap roles. Then write each rule using proper notation, such as f(x) = 2x + 1.

activities.title: Savings Sequence Investigation
activities.materials: a notebook and a moneybox (or a pretend one).
steps: Choose a starting amount and a fixed amount to add each week, like start $5, add $3.
Write the balance for the first six weeks as a sequence.
Find the nth term formula for the balance after n weeks.
Use it to predict the balance after 20 weeks, then check by extending the sequence.

activities.title: Draw a Linear Graph
activities.materials: squared paper, a ruler, and a pencil.
steps: Choose a linear function such as y = 2x + 1.
Make a table of values for x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
Plot each (x, y) pair as a point on the grid.
Join the points with a ruler. Check that they all lie on one straight line.
Then try y = 3x − 2 on the same grid and compare which line is steeper.

activities.title: Real-World Rule Hunt (Family Task)
activities.materials: your family, or your AI tutor if family isn't available, and everyday prices.
steps: Find a real cost with a fixed part and a per-item part, like a taxi fare or a market stall rent.
Write it as a function, for example C(k) = 3 + 2k for a taxi in Mogadishu.
Ask a family member, or your AI tutor, to name a number of kilometres and work out the cost together.
Then reverse it: given a total cost, work backwards to find the number of items.

activities.title: Sequence Detective Challenge
steps: Write a sequence using a two-step rule, like “multiply by 2, then subtract 6”.
Show only the first four terms to a friend, or to your AI tutor if no one else is available.
Challenge them to find your rule and the next term.
Reveal your rule and check whether it works for every term you wrote.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity made the nth term formula clearest? What was the trickiest part of drawing a graph or guessing a rule? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher, parent, or AI tutor at your next session.

rules.title: What a Function Machine Does
rules.text: You will also meet functions. A function is a machine that takes an input, follows a fixed rule, and gives back exactly one output. When Amina works out the cost of a taxi ride across Mogadishu, or when Yusuf predicts how much water is left in the family tank after a number of days, they are using functions, whether they call them that or not. By the end of the unit you will write functions using proper notation such as f(x) = 2x + 3, build tables of values, and draw the straight-line graphs that linear functions produce.

rules.title: Why Sequences and Functions Matter
rules.text: Why does this matter? Sequences and functions are the bridge between the arithmetic you already know and the algebra that unlocks higher mathematics, science, and computing. Traders use sequences to plan savings that grow month by month. Farmers near Hargeisa use functions to estimate how a herd of goats grows over the years. Engineers use them to design staircases, and scientists use them to model how a population of bacteria multiplies. When you can spot a pattern, describe it with a rule, and use that rule to predict, you are thinking like a mathematician about the real world.

rules.title: Generating Sequences from a Rule
rules.text: Generate sequences from a first term and a rule, including multi-step rules.

rules.title: What Is a Sequence?
rules.text: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follows a rule. Each number is called a term, and its place in the line is its position: the first term, the second term, and so on. Look at the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, … The first term is 2, the second term is 5, the third term is 8. The three dots at the end mean the sequence carries on forever, following the same rule.

rules.title: The Term-to-Term Rule
rules.text: The term-to-term rule tells you how to move from one term to the next. For 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 the rule is “add 3”, because 2 + 3 = 5, then 5 + 3 = 8, then 8 + 3 = 11, and so on. A sequence that goes up or down by the same fixed amount every step is called a linear sequence (or arithmetic sequence), and that fixed amount is the common difference.

rules.title: Descending Sequences and Negative Differences
rules.text: Sequences can also go down. Take 20, 17, 14, 11, 8, … Here the rule is “subtract 3”, so the common difference is −3. To find any common difference, subtract a term from the one after it: 17 − 20 = −3. If you always subtract the earlier term from the later term, a rising sequence gives a positive difference and a falling sequence gives a negative one.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find the nth term of 12, 17, 22, 27, 32, … and use it to find the 100th term.
Is 100 a term of the sequence with nth term 3n − 1? Explain using working.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3n − 1 = 100 gives 3n = 101, n = 33.67 — not a whole number, so 100 is not a term.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Which sequence reaches 50 first: A: 2, 5, 8, 11, … or B: 1, 6, 11, 16, …? Justify with nth terms.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A: 3n − 1 = 50 gives n = 17; B: 5n − 4 = 50 gives n = 10.8, so B first passes 50 at the 11th term. B reaches 50 first.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: For the sequence with nth term 5n − 1, find the first term greater than 200.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 5n − 1 > 200 gives 5n > 201, n > 40.2, so n = 41 and the 41st term = 204.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A quadratic function h(x) = x² − 4x + 3. Find h(0), h(3) and h(5).
For the function h(x) = 2x + 4, explain why the points in its table of values always lie on a straight line, and find h(3).
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Each time x increases by 1, h(x) increases by 2 (the coefficient of x), so the output changes by the same fixed amount for every equal step in the input — this constant rate of change is what makes the graph a straight line. h(3) = 2(3) + 4 = 10.

questions.hint: Substitute x = 5 into the rule and work out the output.

questions.question: The graph of y = 2x + 1 passes through which of these points?
questions.hint: Substitute the x-value from each point into the equation and check the y-value.
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 2 into y = 2x + 1: y = 2(2) + 1 = 5, so the point (2, 5) lies on the line.

questions.question: A sequence has nth term 3n + 4. Which of these numbers is a term in the sequence?
questions.hint: Set 3n + 4 equal to each option and check whether n is a whole number.
questions.explanation: 3n + 4 = 22 gives 3n = 18, so n = 6, a whole number — 22 is the 6th term. The other options do not give a whole number for n.

questions.question: Find the next term: 5, 7, 9, 11, ___
questions.hint: Ask yourself what "Sequence" means here before you choose.
questions.explanation: The rule is add 2 each time, so the next term is 11 + 2 = 13.

questions.question: Which nth term formula matches the sequence 2, 6, 10, 14, …?
questions.hint: Find the common difference first, then work out b = first term − common difference.
questions.explanation: Common difference = 4, so a = 4. b = first term − a = 2 − 4 = −2. nth term = 4n − 2. Check: n = 1 gives 4(1) − 2 = 2 ✓.

questions.question: A sequence starts at 10. The rule is “subtract 3, then multiply by 2”. What is the 3rd term?
questions.hint: Apply the rule step by step, following the order given.

questions.question: A dot pattern grows like this: Pattern 1 = 2 dots, Pattern 2 = 5 dots, Pattern 3 = 8 dots. What is the nth term formula for the number of dots?
questions.hint: Find the common difference between patterns, then use it to build the nth term formula.
questions.explanation: Common difference = 3, so a = 3. b = first term − a = 2 − 3 = −1. nth term = 3n − 1. Check: n = 1 gives 3(1) − 1 = 2 ✓.

selfAssessment: I can identify and continue number sequences using term-to-term rules.
I can find and use the nth term formula (of the form an + b) for linear sequences.
I can generate sequences from a first term and a rule, including multi-step rules.
I can connect visual patterns to numerical sequences and find their formulas.
I can use function machines and write functions in the notation f(x) = ….
